kicker: Second-generation restaurant unit · Washington, DC · Surveyed August 2026
h1: The open ceiling the design wanted sat under failing fireproofing.
description: A restaurant unit on New York Avenue, DC: failing fireproofing above the ceiling, a power gap smaller than it looked, and a storefront to price pre-lease.
summary: A national food and beverage brand was weighing a corner restaurant unit in an Art-Deco office building on New York Avenue. Their format calls for an exposed ceiling and plenty of 208 V power. The listing looked like a good second-generation space. One visit showed what it would actually take.

findings.title: Above the tiles, the fireproofing was falling off the steel.
findings.body: The deck and beams carry a sprayed fire-resistive coating. It was cracked, spalled and hanging off in chunks, with hanger rods and cables driven straight through it. On this type of construction that is a code matter, not a cosmetic one, and it sits exactly where an open ceiling would expose it.
findings.action: A specialist fireproofing survey and a remediation price before the ceiling design is fixed.

photos.alt: Sprayed fireproofing broken away from a steel beam above the ceiling, with hanger rods passing through it
photos.caption: Coating detached from the beam, hanger rods driven through it.

photos.alt: Ceiling void showing cracked sprayed fireproofing on the deck above ductwork and cable
photos.caption: The same condition across the plenum, above the ductwork.

findings.title: The power looked short. It wasn't, once we read the nameplates.
findings.body: The unit has a 400 A service at 480 V, which is more capacity than the brand's standard asks for. Everything at 208 V passes through a single 30 kVA transformer, though, and that is roughly a fifth of what the format needs. The panel directory showed plenty of spare ways.
findings.action: A bigger step-down transformer and a new 208 V board, not a new utility service. That is a much smaller and faster job.

photos.alt: Dry-type step-down transformer in the electrical room with its rating plate
photos.caption: The 30 kVA step-down transformer: the real constraint, read from its plate.

findings.title: The storefront needed money too.
findings.body: The full corner storefront is single-pane glazing. The coating at the curved corner had flaked away, the caulk at the pavement had failed, earlier patch repairs had failed in turn and the granite base was drilled and spalled.
findings.action: Price the envelope repairs and the glazing decision alongside the fit-out, not after it.

photos.alt: Granite storefront base at a curved corner with drilled holes and failed sealant at the pavement
photos.caption: Granite base at the corner: drilled holes, failed sealant at the pavement line.

also: Also on the list: water damage under the bar, restrooms that fall short of current accessibility standards, and a full kitchen exhaust system the new format doesn't need. Removing it frees up floor space, but some of that equipment is leased, so ownership has to be checked first. We also identified the 2007 permit set as this space and traced the fourteen missing mechanical, electrical and plumbing sheets to a records request rather than another visit.
delivered: Within the week, the client had a narrative report, a 3D walkthrough, a nameplate-level equipment register and a prioritised list of six cost items to price before signing.
